e.t: This word is a proper name for a person, represented in English as Abigaia. Its listed meanings are “Abigaias” and “Aviyeas,” alternative forms associated with the same personal name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 1 Samuel 25:39 and once in 2 Samuel 3:3. Because it is a name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is primarily the person it identifies, not a quality or action.

This noun means a loop: a curved part used for joining or fastening pieces together. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 11 times, all in Exodus, especially in descriptions of the tabernacle’s curtains and furnishings. The word therefore names a practical loop or ring-like feature rather than an abstract idea. Its exact role in any particular verse depends on the object being described, but its central meaning remains a loop used as part of a constructed item.

This adjective describes someone or something unprincipled—acting without regard for moral standards or rightful order. It identifies a quality rather than an action: the person or thing described is characterized by disregard for what is proper. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the description of an unprincipled character or conduct.

This Greek LXX noun means a “request” or “demand”—something a person asks for or insists upon receiving. It can describe a specific appeal made to another person, whether presented as a humble petition or a firm claim. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in 1 Kings and Job. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and situation. [p03:word:lxx:L700491:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L700491:occurrences]

e.h: Make Less or Be in Need
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “make less; in need.” It describes reduction or a condition in which something is lacking, rather than abundance or fullness. As a verb, it expresses an action or state involving becoming lesser or being in need. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Samuel 2:5 and Jeremiah 51:18. The surrounding verse determines whether the wording emphasizes being reduced or the resulting need.

This verb means “milk”: to draw milk from an animal. It describes an action rather than the milk itself, so it functions as a verb in the Greek Old Testament. The word occurs twice in the LXX, in Job 10:10 and Proverbs 30:33. Its basic meaning remains concrete and straightforward, referring to the act of obtaining milk. The surrounding verse supplies the particular comparison or purpose, but the word itself identifies the milking action.

This adjective describes someone or something as flawless and blameless—without a defect that would make it unacceptable. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used especially for offerings and people who are to meet an unstated standard of wholeness or uprightness. The word occurs 83 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures represented here, with many occurrences in Leviticus and Numbers. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what person or thing is being described.

This Greek LXX verb means “boil well” or “seethe.” It describes vigorous boiling or agitation, whether referring to something heated until it bubbles strongly or to a comparable forceful churning. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Nahum and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains intense boiling or seething rather than quiet warmth.

This Greek LXX verb means “raise up”—to lift something or someone upward. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, once in Nahum and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of raising up. The word is found in Nahum 1:5 and 1 Maccabees 7:24.

This verb means to bring something about—to “effect” or “achieve” it. It describes accomplishing a purpose or producing a result, rather than merely intending or attempting one. In the Greek LXX represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 9:12. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, its precise force in that passage must be read from its sentence and context.

This verb means to disown or reject someone or something—to refuse acceptance, recognition, or continued association. It describes an active turning away rather than simple uncertainty or neglect. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including uses rendered “reject.” The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but the central idea remains refusal: treating someone or something as unacceptable, unwanted, or no longer acknowledged.

This Greek verb means “roll away”: to move something from its place by rolling it. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Genesis 29, where its basic sense concerns rolling something away. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word’s central idea remains the physical removal or shifting of something through rolling.

Arama is a proper name, referring to a specific named person, family, or group rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Ezra 2:26 and Nehemiah 7:30. Without the surrounding verse text, the precise identity signified by the name cannot be stated more narrowly. Its meaning is therefore the name itself: Arama.

Aria is a proper name: it identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 15:25, and is rendered as “Aria.” Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, the name itself does not establish the person’s role, character, or significance in that passage. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name Aria, with the specific identification supplied by the verse’s context.

This word is a proper name identifying a person: “Arōdaios; Arotheos.” It is not a general description or action word, but a personal designation used to distinguish one individual. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:25. The name’s precise significance beyond identifying that person is not explained by the available lexical information or reference alone.

Assares is a proper name, referring to a specifically named person or place rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, at Joshua 15:10. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise referent cannot be identified more specifically from the name alone. The spelling functions as a name preserved in the Greek LXX text, not as a common descriptive word.

This verb means to act in an indecent way—behaving improperly or without due regard for what is fitting. It describes conduct rather than a person’s name or status, and it can be applied to actions viewed as shameful or dishonorable. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in five Old Testament verses: once in Deuteronomy and four times in Ezekiel. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX adverb means “tomorrow” or “next day,” pointing to the day immediately after the present one. It describes when something will happen, be done, or be expected, rather than naming a person, object, or action. The word occurs 61 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing a consistent time reference across its uses. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary meaning remains a future day immediately following today.

In the Greek Old Testament, this word means “agate,” a noun naming a particular stone. It occurs three times in the LXX: twice in Exodus and once in Ezekiel, at Exodus 28:19, Exodus 36:19, and Ezekiel 28:13. These references identify the word’s normal lexical sense as the name of the stone itself, rather than an action, quality, or person. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse context.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Baithsamysitos” or “Vethsamisitos.” It identifies a particular named person, place, or group rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 6:18. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide enough context to determine more specifically what or whom it identifies. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, not to the name alone.

This noun means “palm rod,” referring to a rod or staff made from, or associated with, a palm tree. It names a tangible object rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Maccabees 13:37. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise use in that sentence cannot be described further. Its basic meaning remains a palm rod: a palm-related staff or slender branch used as an object.

This word is a proper name referring to a person named “Bērsaphēs,” also identified as “Virsafis.” It functions as a personal designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Joshua 19:21. The available record identifies the name, but without the verse text it does not establish additional meaning, significance, or details about the person.

This Greek LXX noun means “farmers,” referring to people who cultivate and work the land. It is a straightforward occupational term rather than a description of a spiritual quality or symbolic idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 25:12. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific situation in which the word appears, but its ordinary meaning is simply people engaged in farming or cultivation.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Gaithan; Yethan.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it appears only once, at 1 Kings 5:11, so its lexical meaning is simply the personal name itself. The two forms are presented as name variants, not as separate concepts.

This Greek LXX particle means “in fact.” It adds emphasis to a statement, drawing attention to its truth or particular force. Rather than naming a person, action, or object, it helps shape how the surrounding words are understood. The particle appears 167 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, so its exact emphasis depends on the sentence where it occurs.

This noun means “public worker,” referring to a person who works in a public role or service. It presents the person by the kind of work performed for the broader community, rather than by a private occupation or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs two times, in Wisdom 15:13 and 2 Maccabees 4:1. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains a worker serving in a public capacity.

This Greek LXX verb means “bear twins,” describing the act of giving birth to two offspring at once. It is a specific word for twin-bearing rather than a general term for birth. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Song of Songs, at Song of Songs 4:2 and 6:6. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, those references establish where the word appears but do not by themselves explain the full poetic picture in each passage.

This verb means “see through” or “see clearly,” describing the act of perceiving something plainly rather than merely looking at it. It can express clear recognition or discernment in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Job 6:19; the available information identifies its normal lexical sense but does not provide the verse text needed to explain its particular use there.

This Greek LXX noun means “runaway”: a person who has fled or escaped from a place, duty, authority, or former situation. It identifies the person by the fact of fleeing, rather than describing the act of running itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 8:35. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the precise force of the reference cannot be stated beyond this basic lexical meaning.

Edania, also rendered Ethania, is a proper name—the name of a person or family rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Nehemiah 10:17. Because the word functions as a name, its meaning is primarily its identification of the person or family it designates; the surrounding verse is needed to identify that individual or household more specifically.

This noun means “conviction”: a firm sense that something is true, right, or established. It can describe the inward certainty or compelling judgment produced by recognizing what is true. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 39 times, especially in Proverbs and Job, where matters of wisdom, speech, and accountability are prominent. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains conviction—an assured judgment rather than a passing impression.

Elisai, also rendered Elise, is a proper name identifying a person. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Ezekiel 27:7. The name itself identifies the person but does not, by its lexical meaning alone, describe a quality, action, or teaching. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being mentioned there.

This verb means “filled with,” describing someone or something becoming full of a particular substance, quality, or influence. It expresses the result or condition of being filled, rather than simply an empty space being occupied. The word appears once in the Greek Septuagint, in 3 Maccabees 5:42. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

This verb means to set oneself against someone or something—to oppose it. It describes active resistance rather than simple disagreement, presenting a person or force as standing in opposition. In the LXX material represented here, it occurs twice: once in 3 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines who is opposing whom and what form that resistance takes, but the word itself centers on being set against or acting in opposition.

This Greek LXX verb means “march out” or “depart this life.” It describes going out or leaving, and it can be used for a person's death as a departure from earthly life. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish writings represented in this corpus: once in Judges and twice in 1 and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adverb means “fitting” or “suitable.” It describes something done or expressed in an appropriate way—something that matches the situation rather than being out of place. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 9:27. The reference identifies its sole occurrence, but the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

gl: add to by mixing; mix with
d: add to by mixing; mix with

e.t: This verb means “add to by mixing” or “mix with.” It describes combining something with something else rather than keeping it separate. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs two times, showing a specific action of joining or blending. Its exact force in Proverbs 14:10 and Ezekiel 16:37 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains the addition of one thing into another through mixing.

This Greek LXX noun means “strength,” referring to power or force. It presents strength as a quality or condition rather than an action. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains focused and consistent: the capacity to stand firm, act powerfully, or possess might. The surrounding verse is needed to show whether the word emphasizes physical, military, or broader strength in a particular occurrence.

This adjective describes someone who is approachable, pleasant, and courteous in dealing with others. It presents a person as friendly rather than harsh or difficult to meet. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:9; the verse’s surrounding wording would be needed to explain the particular nuance there. Its central meaning remains a gracious, agreeable manner toward other people.

This adjective describes something with a fine purple border or edging. It points to a decorative feature whose distinctive quality is the carefully finished purple trim, rather than naming the object itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Ezekiel 23:12. Its precise reference there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its lexical sense remains focused on an item marked by an elegant purple border.

This adjective describes someone or something connected with being on horseback or riding. It identifies a mounted person or rider rather than describing walking or standing on foot. In the Greek text represented here, the word occurs three times: twice in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what or whom it modifies.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to foster or care for someone or something. It describes providing attentive support and nourishment rather than merely being present. As a verb, it expresses an action of tending, cherishing, or looking after what needs care. It occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in passages from Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, and Job. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains active, sustaining care.

gl: that which is laid down and established; law
d: that which is laid down and established; law

e.t: This noun means “that which is laid down and established; law”—a rule, ordinance, or standard set in place with authority. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, it appears five times, including in Proverbs, Wisdom, and Maccabees. Its basic focus is something established to guide conduct or regulate life, rather than a passing suggestion. The surrounding passage determines whether the word points to a particular law or to established laws more generally.

This adjective means “eaten by beasts,” describing something that has been consumed by wild animals. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, in Genesis 44:28. The word’s meaning is specific and concrete: it identifies the condition of a person or thing reported to have been devoured by animals. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains clear.

This word is a proper name identifying a person known as “Iair; Ier.” It is not a common word describing an action, quality, object, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 12 times across 10 verses, beginning in Numbers and continuing through later historical books. Because it functions as a personal name, its meaning in any particular verse depends chiefly on which person named Iair is being mentioned and on the surrounding passage.

Ieteba, also rendered “Ieteva,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Kings 21:19. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its particular role in that passage cannot be described further, but its basic meaning is its identity as a name.

This proper name refers to “Ioudaia,” also rendered in the lexical definition as “Iuthea.” It functions as a name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 94 times, appearing in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. The name is found across historical, poetic, and prophetic writings, so its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iōanou” or “Ioanu.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 28:12. The available information establishes the name’s form and function, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person named there. Its precise reference is therefore determined by that passage’s context.

This word is a proper name: “Iōēl; Iil.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 23 times across 23 verses in the LXX corpus, especially in genealogical and historical passages, and it also appears as the name of the prophet Joel. The exact person identified depends on the surrounding verse, since the same personal name can belong to more than one individual.

This noun means “cleanliness”: the quality or condition of being clean. It names cleanliness as a state or characteristic rather than describing an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:24. Its lexical sense remains focused and concrete: it identifies cleanliness itself, while the surrounding verse would determine how that idea functions in its particular setting.

This adjective describes someone who is ill-minded or malicious—whose thinking or intent is harmful rather than good. It points to a settled quality of character, not merely an isolated mistake or moment of weakness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Proverbs, so its recorded use is limited but consistent. The surrounding verse is needed to show exactly how this description applies in each passage.

Kariathaim, also rendered Kariathem, is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears five times in the Greek Old Testament, in passages from Numbers, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, and Jeremiah. Because the supplied material gives no verse text or surrounding context, its precise significance in each passage must be understood from the passage itself. The name’s meaning is therefore its identification of Kariathaim or Kariathem as a distinct biblical place-name.

This word refers to mockery or derision—the scornful treatment of someone through ridicule or contempt. It can function as a noun for the act or condition of being mocked, and its use can also serve adverbially to describe something done in a mocking manner. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice, in Psalms and 1 Maccabees. Its central idea remains the same: treating a person or matter with insulting scorn rather than respect.

This preposition means “face to face” or “before,” describing something positioned directly in front of someone or occurring in that person’s presence. In the Greek Old Testament, it can mark a direct position or presence rather than an action by itself. It occurs five times in the LXX, chiefly in Joshua, and is rendered “before” in several instances. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is physical position or being in someone’s presence.

This Greek LXX noun means “heat”—the condition of warmth or intense hotness. It can describe the heat experienced in ordinary life, including exposure to severe conditions. The word occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, appearing from Genesis through Baruch. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: physical heat or burning warmth, while the surrounding verse determines how that heat affects people, places, or circumstances.

This Greek noun means “danger”: a threatening situation or serious risk that may harm a person or group. It can refer to one peril or to dangers in the plural. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures represented here, it occurs 11 times, showing ordinary use for circumstances that place people in jeopardy. Its exact force in any verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to the distribution of land or to an inherited portion of land—what is assigned as someone’s heritage. It can describe land received or allotted rather than merely land viewed as property. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages from Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Daniel, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is an allotted inheritance or the act of assigning land.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut” or “mourn.” It can describe physically cutting something, and it can also express mourning or grief. The surrounding passage determines which sense is intended. The word occurs 85 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so both meanings belong to its normal range rather than being a rare usage. It appears especially often in prophetic and historical books, where cutting and mourning are recurring actions or responses.

This word means “parsley,” referring to a particular herb. As a noun, it names the plant rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Isaiah 28, appearing in two verses. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical meaning remains the name of this herb.

Laban is a personal name referring to a man named Laban. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears 58 times, all in Genesis, and is consistently rendered “Laban.” Because it is a proper name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is primarily the identification of this individual. The name appears from Genesis 24 through Genesis 46, including references in Genesis 24:29, Genesis 27:43, and Genesis 29. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “receipt.” It refers to receiving something or to the acknowledgment that something has been received. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here: twice in Proverbs and twice in Sirach. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains the receiving or acknowledgment of what has been given or delivered.

This noun refers to a stone-mason or engraver—someone whose work involves shaping or engraving stone. It identifies a worker by his skilled craft rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Sirach 45:11. Its meaning is therefore a specific occupational designation for a person who works with stone, whether by construction, carving, or inscription.

Malach, also rendered Malakh, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 9:41. The available wording identifies the person by name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text here to explain his family connection, role, or significance. Its meaning is therefore best stated simply as the personal name Malach or Malakh.

Machamas, also rendered Makhamas, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at Nehemiah 11:31. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding passage and the corresponding biblical context.

gl: weaver’s beam; beam of a loom
d: weaver’s beam; beam of a loom

e.t: This noun means a “weaver’s beam” or “beam of a loom”—the substantial wooden part of a loom used in weaving. It names an ordinary tool or piece of equipment rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 17:7. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete: a structural beam belonging to a loom, understood through the everyday work of making cloth.

This noun refers to “eating alone” and can also describe “gluttony,” or excessive eating. It names a practice or appetite rather than an action word. Its central idea is solitary or excessive eating. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 1:27. That reference identifies its only occurrence, but without the verse text, the precise force of the word in that sentence cannot be stated beyond this basic meaning.

Mōdein, also rendered Mothin, is a proper name for a place. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographic name used in the Greek Old Testament corpus. The name occurs nine times, in nine verses: eight occurrences are in 1 Maccabees and one is in 2 Maccabees. Because the word identifies a location, its specific significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the people or events associated with that place.

Napheta, also rendered Nafeta, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 17:11. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine whether it identifies a person, place, or another named entity; that role must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “renovate” or “renew”: to make something new again or restore it. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Jeremiah 4:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense is the work of renewing or restoring something so that it is fresh and usable again.

This Greek LXX noun means a “slip” or “fall”—a misstep, stumble, or downward falling. It can describe a literal fall or, depending on the passage, the idea of going astray or suffering a collapse. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, especially in Psalms and Jeremiah. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a failure of footing or a fall from a secure position.

This noun means “likeness”: a form, image, or representation that resembles something else. In the Greek Old Testament, it commonly identifies a visible resemblance or an image made to represent a living thing or object. It occurs 41 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, with especially frequent use in Ezekiel and Deuteronomy. The word itself describes resemblance; the surrounding passage determines whether that likeness is being described, made, seen, or forbidden.

gl: bird which migrates with the quails
d: bird which migrates with the quails

e.t: This noun means “bird which migrates with the quails.” It refers to a bird associated with the seasonal movement of quails, rather than simply naming any bird. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs six times, including passages connected with Exodus, Numbers, Psalms, and Wisdom. Its English renderings usually identify quails, while the fuller meaning points to the kind of bird and its migratory association.

Ophni is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly its role as a personal name. The name occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, all in 1 Samuel, from 1 Samuel 1:3 through 4:11. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further lexical meaning beyond identifying Ophni.

This Greek LXX noun means “plaything,” referring to something used for amusement or play. It appears twice in the Greek text preserved in Wisdom, in Wisdom 12:26 and Wisdom 15:12. The word itself identifies an object as a toy or source of play, while the surrounding passage determines whether it is being mentioned literally or used as part of a comparison. Its meaning is therefore simple and concrete: a thing treated as an object of play rather than as something serious or useful for another purpose.

This noun means “tradition”: something handed down and preserved as an established teaching or practice. It refers to what has been transmitted from earlier people or generations, rather than something newly introduced. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs twice, both in Jeremiah, so its normal sense is clear even though the available information does not include the surrounding verse text. Its precise force in either passage depends on the immediate context.

This verb means “keep silent”: to remain quiet or refrain from speaking. It describes silence as an action or restraint rather than simply indicating that no sound is present. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 19 times across 18 verses, including passages in Genesis, Numbers, 1 Samuel, Psalms, Hosea, and Habakkuk. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on who is silent and what speech or response the surrounding passage requires.

This adjective means “belonging to one’s father.” It describes something associated with, connected to, or received from a father. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears 161 times, so it can describe a recurring relationship to a father rather than a single isolated situation. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains connection or belonging to one’s father.

gl: looked at from all sides; admired of all observers
d: looked at from all sides; admired of all observers

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something that is looked at from all sides and admired by those who observe it. It presents an object of broad attention and favorable regard, rather than merely something noticed briefly. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Proverbs 31:23, so its normal meaning is clear from its stated definition, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular force in that passage.

This noun refers to “over-exactness”: an excessive concern with being precise or exact. It describes more than ordinary care; it points to exactness carried too far. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 41:24. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is clear: an extreme or undue insistence on exactness rather than a balanced use of care and precision.

This verb means to make faithful—to establish or cause someone or something to remain dependable and true. It describes an action that produces faithfulness rather than merely recognizing it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times, including passages concerning God’s enduring promises and the reliability of what he establishes. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains making faithful or dependable.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a great multitude—a large crowd or gathering of people. It describes many people considered together rather than one individual. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical Greek text preserved in this corpus: twice in Job and once in Baruch. Its basic sense remains consistent across these occurrences: a numerous crowd or mass of people. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points plainly to a large gathering.
